# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Assessment of the 24-month Varden/Halden follow-up (VC-2023-04-F)

This is a strong follow-up that settles much of the earlier dispute. It meets the standards Varga and Holm themselves set: randomisation, record-based output, actual hours and long follow-up. It tests the meetings hypothesis under a registered plan, adds a hours measure that doesn't depend on timesheets, and checks the meta-analysis's long-follow-up studies, which turned out to be exactly the weak designs I suspected. The authors are generally careful, especially about the Halden survivors and the control-office meeting audit.

There are still several problems: one headline comparison mixes two measures, one plausible bias isn't mentioned, the "confirms" language overstates the mediation result, and the hours measure isn't defined.

## Arithmetic checks

- Timesheets at 24 months: 0.966/0.88 = **+9.8%** ✓
- System logs at 24 months: 0.966/0.89 = **+8.5%** ✓
- Halden continuers: 34.9/40.3 = 0.866 (−13.4%); 96.8/86.6 = **+11.8%** ✓
- Counter staffing: restoring output from 0.886 per worker needs 1/0.886 ≈ **+13% staff**, so the county's "12% more" is plausible. The +9% cost per contact implies staff are about three-quarters of cost. That's reasonable but not stated.

## What it settles

**1. The "entirely an artifact" claim is refuted.** A randomised trial with record-based output, log-measured hours and two years of follow-up finds +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The authors' summary is fair: Varga and Holm were right about the measurement problems and wrong about the conclusion.

**2. The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim is refuted.** All four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. In the one controlled long study, the gain declined.

**3. Coverage-bound work: the counter arm was ended at month 12.** Waits are now compared against control (7.3 vs 4.0 minutes), which fixes my earlier complaint that wait times had no control comparison. This is the clearest real-world test so far, and the scheme failed it.

**4. The size of the per-hour gain is now consistent across sources.** Varden gives 8.5–9.8%, the controlled studies in the meta-analysis 8–10%, and corrected Halden about 11–12%, which is an upper bound.

## Problems

**1. The headline compares different hours measures.** The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data". But 12.5% is a timesheet figure, and the 9-month log column is blank. The like-for-like decline is 12.5% → 9.8%, a fall of about 22%, not 32%. The body gets this right, but the summary and Section 5 ("declined by about a quarter") should use the same comparison. Also, the 9- and 24-month confidence intervals overlap heavily, so the decline itself is not statistically established.

**2. The control-office meeting audit biases the 24-month estimate toward decay.** The authors report it only as a hint about mechanism. But two of seven control offices raised their output per hour by about 4% from month 15. That lifts the control comparison, so the difference-in-differences understates the treatment effect at 24 months. If offices are roughly equal in size, the control average would rise by around 1 point, which could explain a third or more of the 2.7-point "decline". It may also be spillover from treated offices, the contamination that office-level randomisation was meant to prevent. A sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices is needed before reading the change from 12.5% to 9.8% as fading.

**3. Two time points can't distinguish a plateau from steady decline.** At 2.7 points per 15 months, a straight-line trend would reach zero around year 6. That projection is as unjustified as Varga and Holm's month-10 projection, but the data don't rule it out either. The county's case-management system logs cases continuously, so a month-by-month trajectory should be possible. It is the most informative analysis still missing.

**4. The log-in measure needs defining, and it matters for the mediation result.**
- "Active log-in time on the case-management system" presumably excludes meetings, email and other work outside the system. If so, it is not total working time.
- Rough arithmetic: treated offices cut meetings by about 3.3 hours a week more than controls, and total hours fell by about 4.5 hours. If logs excluded meeting time, case-system hours would have fallen by only about 4%, not 11%. So either logs include meeting time (being logged in while in a meeting), or something else is going on.
- This affects the mediation outcome, "output per log-measured hour". If log hours exclude meetings, cutting meetings can't raise output per log hour by removing unproductive time. It could only work by reducing interruptions.
- The log measure was added at follow-up. Was pre-period log data available for the difference-in-differences baseline?
- A cross-check gives a different picture. Using timesheets, non-meeting hours in treated offices were about 29.5 against 30.9 in control, and output per FTE was −3.4%. Output per *non-meeting* hour is then roughly +1%. That suggests meeting time could account for nearly all of the gain, not 47%. The gap between these two estimates is probably about definitions, and it needs explaining.

**5. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result.**
- The test was pre-registered, but in the same seven treated offices that generated the hypothesis. It is a pre-specified re-test, not an independent replication.
- "A larger sample of office-months" adds little, because office-months within an office are not independent. The effective sample is still 7 vs 7 clusters, and with so few clusters the 28–66% interval may be too narrow.
- Meeting cuts and lower fatigue are likely linked: fewer meetings could mean less fatigue. A 47/18/35 split assumes the pathways add up separately, which may not hold.
- The authors note the no-confounding assumption in their limitations. The summary should say "supports" rather than "confirms".

Even so, a pre-specified test in which meetings outweigh fatigue more than twofold is a meaningful result. It reverses the original Halden authors' guess that fatigue was the main explanation.

**6. The Halden subset is selected twice over.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded, and those that declined may have done worse. The authors call the result an upper bound, which is right, and there is still no control group across two years of other changes. One notable detail: one of the three reverters was a **marketing agency** citing client deadlines, which is nominally discretionary work. That suggests coverage constraints come from obligations to clients, not from sector, which supports the meta-analysis's point that the binary classification is crude. It also shows reversion continued after the original 92% continuation figure.

**7. Still not addressed:**
- **Sick days (−27%).** Whether the schedule was four days or five shorter days is still unstated, so the mechanical effect of fewer working days can't be excluded.
- **Cost in case-processing.** Paid overtime and output per FTE drifting to −3.4% suggest cost per case rose. A county needs that figure.
- **Independence.** Okafor co-authors the follow-up of his own pilot, and the Varden team evaluates its own hypothesis. Pre-registration helps, but independent replication would be better.

## Where the five documents leave things

| Question | Current best reading |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | About 8–10% per actual hour at two years in the best evidence. Real and lasting at least two years. |
| Decay | Some decline from 9 to 24 months is likely but not precisely sized; it may be partly an artifact of the control-office audit. Longer-run path unknown. |
| Per-worker output, discretionary | About −3%: mostly but not fully offset. |
| Coverage-bound work | Fails without extra staff: about 12% more staff and about +9% cost per contact to restore service. |
| Mechanism | Cutting meetings is the largest identified pathway; fatigue is secondary; about a third unexplained. Single site; not independently replicated. |
| "Sector-general" / "entirely artifact" / "no decay" | All three rejected. |

## The open question

The authors identify it themselves: whether reorganising alone captures most of the gain, or whether cutting hours is what forces reorganisation and makes it stick. The control-office audit (+4.1% from a smaller meeting cut, with no hours change) is suggestive. Answering it needs a three-arm trial comparing reduced hours, meeting and process reorganisation without an hours change, and control, with month-by-month output and a clearly defined hours measure. Until then, an employer's cheapest first step is probably a meeting audit, with reduced hours as a possible addition.
